API Conventions

Source: vignettes/articles/api-conventions.Rmd
api-conventions.Rmd

This page is the contract for how tidycreel’s functions are named, what they take and what they return. It is written for two readers: users, who should be able to guess a function’s name and arguments from its job, and contributors, who add functions without making the first reader’s guess wrong.

A rule here that a test can check is checked, by tests/testthat/test-api-conventions.R. Where the package does not yet meet a rule, the test carries the gap as a named exception with the issue that tracks it, and fails if an exception is no longer needed. The exception list can only shrink.

The shape of an analysis

Every design-based analysis has the same shape:

design <- creel_design(calendar, date = date, strata = day_type) |>  # 1. structure
  add_counts(counts, count_col = n_anglers) |>                       # 2. data
  add_interviews(interviews, catch = catch_total, effort = hours,
                 trip_status = trip_status)

est <- estimate_effort(design, by = day_type)                        # 3. estimate
est |> tibble::as_tibble()                                           # 4. use (#476)
  1. creel_design() describes how the season was sampled. It is the only constructor; the survey type is an argument, not a different function.
  2. add_*() attaches one kind of observation and returns the design, so the steps pipe.
  3. estimate_*() turns the design into an estimate with a standard error and a confidence interval.
  4. The result prints, plots with autoplot(), and converts to a plain tibble.

New functions fit one of these steps or one of the families below. A function that fits none is a sign it belongs in a different package, or that the design of the feature needs discussing in an issue first.

Function families

The prefix says what the function does. Within a family, the first argument is the same kind of object.

Prefix Job First argument Returns
creel_design() Construct a design calendar creel_design
add_*() Attach observations to a design design creel_design
prep_*() Reshape raw field data into what an add_*() takes data data frame
estimate_*() Design-based estimate with uncertainty design creel_estimates
summarize_*() Unexpanded description of the sample design data frame
validate_*(), check_*() Check inputs; report problems the thing checked a report
generate_*() Build a sampling schedule or count times schedule inputs schedule
creel_n_*() Plan sample sizes before a season planning numbers numbers
compare_*() Compare estimators, designs or variance methods the things compared a comparison
simulate_*() Simulated data for planning and testing simulation settings data frame
get_*() Read a component out of a design design data frame
as_*() Convert a design to another package’s object design that object
write_*(), read_*() Files the object / the path —
autoplot() Plot a result the result ggplot
theme_creel(), creel_palette() Plot styling style settings a theme / colours

Spelling: summarize, not summarise, in function names.

A few estimate_*() functions are calculators: they take summary numbers (estimate_angler_n(), estimate_exploitation_rate()) or another estimate (estimate_mr_harvest(), estimate_angler_trips(), estimate_effort_per_acre()) rather than a design. They are listed as exceptions in the test so that a new calculator is a deliberate choice.

Known gaps. The first three are listed as exceptions in the test; the last is a mismatch of meaning that a name check cannot see, and is recorded here only:

  • est_*() and estimate_*() coexist (#477).
  • Planning functions use several patterns besides creel_n_*(): creel_power() and power_creel(), optimal_n(), cv_from_n(), reallocate_strata().
  • About twenty data-preparation, scheduling and diagnostic helpers sit outside any family (compute_effort(), standardize_species(), attach_count_times(), audit_strata(), …). Each is listed in the test with its reason.
  • validate_design() plans a sample size; it does not validate a creel_design.

Arguments

Order. The object being worked on comes first (design, then the data being attached), so every step pipes. Options come after the data.

Shared argument names. These mean the same thing everywhere they appear, and appear in this relative order:

Argument Meaning
by Grouping columns, as bare names (by = c(day_type, species))
variance "taylor", "bootstrap" or "jackknife"
conf_level Confidence level, default 0.95
target What the estimate totals over ("sampled_days", …)

Do not add a synonym (level, group, strata_var) for one of these.

Columns are bare names. Arguments that name a column take it unquoted (date = date, count_col = n_anglers) and are resolved with tidyselect, which also accepts a string. Documentation and examples use bare names.

Two spellings of column arguments exist today: a bare role name (creel_design(date = ), add_interviews(catch = , effort = )) and a _col suffix (add_counts(count_col = ), add_sections(section_col = )). The rule for new arguments is open (#479). Until it is settled, match the function you are extending.

Column names are never assumed. The package ships no organisation’s field names. A column is named by the user through an argument or creel_schema(), inferred from the data’s structure where only one column can qualify (as add_counts() does when count_col is omitted and exactly one non-design numeric column remains; with two or more it refuses rather than pick), or created by the package. Examples name the column anyway, so the reader sees which one is used.

Results

Estimates are creel_estimates objects: a tibble of estimates plus the metadata that says what the numbers mean (method, estimator, variance method, confidence level, unit, standard-error components). The metadata travels beside the table rather than in attributes on it, because an ordinary select() or filter() drops attributes without telling anyone.

Every result class must convert with as_tibble() and as.data.frame(), and the conversion copies the metadata a reader needs into columns (#476). A result that cannot leave the package as data is not finished.

Units are derived, never declared. A unit comes from the data’s own definition (party-hours vs angler-hours, a period length, h_open). When it cannot be derived it is NA, meaning unknown. There is no default unit.

NA, NULL and zero are different. A standard-error component that does not apply is NULL; one that applies but is unknown is NA; zero means a known zero. Never report 0 for “not propagated”.

Refuse rather than guess. When the data cannot support an estimate (unsampled strata, units that do not combine, a design the estimator does not cover), stop with an error that says what is missing and how to supply it. Do not drop records, impute, or fall back to a different estimator silently.

Messages

  • Errors, warnings and messages use cli (cli::cli_abort(), cli::cli_warn(), cli::cli_inform()), with the argument or column named in {.arg} / {.field} markup.
  • Errors a caller may want to catch carry a class from the creel_error_* family (creel_error_invalid_input, creel_error_schema_validation, …).
  • Every warning carries a class, creel_warning_<fact>, and the parent creel_warning, so a caller can handle one warning for one call (?creel_warnings lists them). A fact raised in several places uses one class. A tier-3 message carries creel_message_<fact> and the parent creel_message in the same way.
  • A warning should be rare enough to read. Every warning has a tier (?creel_warnings). Information (tier 3) is not a warning: raise it with the internal creel_inform(), as a message with a creel_message_<fact> class, and it is recorded like a warning. A data-quality warning (tier 2) prints once per design: later repeats on the same design are recorded on the result, readable with get_warnings(), but not printed. A warning that the estimate may be wrong (tier 1) prints every time. Raise warnings with the internal creel_warn(), which records them and handles the repeats; do not use .frequency, which hid repeats on a different design for the rest of the session. A test fails if either rule is broken.
  • Examples, vignettes and the README run without warnings, unless the page is demonstrating the warning. A documentation page that warns teaches readers to ignore warnings.

Code style

  • Base pipe |> (the package requires R >= 4.1). Not %>%.
  • tidyverse style: snake_case for functions, arguments and columns.
  • Every export has roxygen documentation with a runnable example, and is listed in _pkgdown.yml.

Adding a function: checklist

  1. Which step or family is it? Use that prefix and that first argument.
  2. Reuse the shared argument names and their order.
  3. Columns as bare names; no assumed column names.
  4. Return the family’s type. A new result class gets as_tibble(), as.data.frame(), print() and format() methods.
  5. Units derived; NA/NULL/zero kept distinct; refuse rather than guess.
  6. Example runs warning-free.
  7. tests/testthat/test-api-conventions.R passes without adding an exception. If it needs one, the PR says why and links an issue.
